concept: Motor fluctuations, wearing-off and dyskinesia management

claims.text: Motor fluctuations are transitions between ON, when levodopa provides useful symptomatic benefit, and OFF, when responsive symptoms re-emerge and function declines. (low confidence)
NICE recommendation 1.3.9 advises seeking Parkinson’s specialist advice before modifying therapy when dyskinesia or motor fluctuations, including wearing-off, develop. (low confidence)

NICE advises considering amantadine when dyskinesia is not adequately managed by modifying existing therapy; the Aradi–Hauser review likewise includes it among options for peak-dose dyskinesia. (medium confidence)

The 2025 MDS review assessed OFF-time, ON-time, motor impairment, disability, health-related quality of life and adverse effects; these outcomes should be distinguished when interpreting treatment benefit. (low confidence)

Wearing-off is gradual loss of dose benefit before the next dose; sudden OFF can be unrelated to dose timing, delayed ON means unusually slow benefit after a dose, and dose failure means no benefit from that dose. These are distinct response patterns. (low confidence)

NICE advises against deep brain stimulation when best medical therapy adequately controls symptoms, and recommends considering it when advanced disease is not adequately controlled; the MDS review also describes escalation when less invasive options provide insufficient benefit. (medium confidence)

When dyskinesia and OFF coexist on immediate-release carbidopa–levodopa, smaller individual doses given more frequently (fractionation) may help reduce peak–trough fluctuations; this is an option rather than a guaranteed response. (low confidence)

For fluctuations inadequately controlled by oral medication, infusion therapies can be considered; the MDS review supports selected continuous-delivery treatments as likely efficacious, rather than guaranteeing benefit for every patient. (medium confidence)

Peak-dose dyskinesia occurs at the peak of the levodopa response; diphasic dyskinesia occurs as levodopa levels rise and fall. Painful dystonia can also occur during OFF, particularly early morning OFF. (low confidence)

A common initial strategy for wearing-off is to shorten the interval between levodopa doses. Practical schedule adjustments are widely used, but the 2025 MDS review notes that not all have been tested in randomized trials. (medium confidence)

For dyskinesia without OFF time, the Aradi–Hauser review suggests considering lower individual levodopa doses or reducing adjunctive medication. This recommendation is explicitly for that response pattern. (low confidence)

If schedule adjustments do not sufficiently improve motor fluctuations, additional medical treatment may be needed; persistent inadequate control can prompt consideration of pump therapy or a neurosurgical procedure. (medium confidence)

NICE NG71 lists the person's individual clinical circumstances (for example symptoms, comorbidities and risks from polypharmacy), their lifestyle circumstances, preferences, needs and goals, and the potential benefits and harms of the different drug classes among its considerations in choosing treatment; the MDS review states that safety and individual tolerability must be taken into account together with each patient's preference. (medium confidence)

The 2025 MDS review used a literature search conducted on January 1, 2023 and required randomized trials with at least three months of follow-up. Its evidence conclusions are therefore bounded by that search and eligibility criteria. (low confidence)

The 2025 MDS review explicitly states that its efficacy designations do not prioritize treatment order or establish larger benefit for an “efficacious” treatment than for a “likely efficacious” treatment. It also notes few long-term comparative studies to guide the first treatment choice. (low confidence)

The MDS review illustrates that OFF-time reduction does not necessarily translate into a clinically meaningful improvement in disability or quality of life: its extended-release levodopa comparison improved OFF/ON outcomes but did not reach clinical relevance for those broader outcomes. (low confidence)

The motor-complications review describes no significant difference in motor-complication rates at 80 weeks in a trial comparing immediate levodopa initiation with a 40-week delay; this finding does not establish that longer delays prevent complications. (low confidence)

narrative.documentConcept: Motor fluctuations, wearing-off and dyskinesia management
narrative.text: Motor fluctuations divide the day into periods of useful medication benefit (ON) and returning symptoms (OFF). Wearing-off, delayed ON, sudden OFF and dose failure represent different patterns; peak-dose and diphasic dyskinesia also differ in their timing. Management requires specialist assessment and balancing symptom control against involuntary movements. Common approaches include adjusting dose intervals, reducing individual doses when appropriate, and escalating treatment when control remains inadequate. Coexisting dyskinesia and OFF may require fractionation rather than simply reducing medication. Patient goals, tolerability, disability and quality of life matter alongside time-based outcomes. The 2025 MDS evidence categories describe strength of evidence and should not be interpreted as a treatment sequence.
